Headline: “Intégrisme”: the career of a word in the Ivorian press, 1985–2016
Text: This interactive timeline traces how the word intégrisme (integrism) was applied to the Muslims of Côte d’Ivoire during the democratic transition of the 1990s, through press articles and Islamic periodicals from the Islam West Africa Collection (IWAC). It follows the accusations made by the government and its press, the responses of the opposition and of Francophone Muslim intellectuals, and the later shift to the vocabulary of terrorism. In the collection, 188 Ivorian articles use the word; 145 of them date from 1992 to 1995.

Headline: “One cannot speak of integrism in Côte d’Ivoire”
Text:
Before multiparty politics, the word intégrisme rarely appeared in the Ivorian press, and almost always to describe something happening elsewhere. In June 1985, Ivoire Dimanche quoted El Hadj Souleymane Doumbia of Ivorian Television: “One cannot speak of integrism in Côte d’Ivoire”. In December 1986, the fourth congress of the AEEMCI asked that “any conflation of Islam, integrism and terrorism” be avoided. The tone changed in August 1991, a year after the return to multiparty politics. After a lecture at the town hall of Attécoubé, where the speaker, Kipré Mohamed, called on Muslims to create “their own institutions, political organisations and unions”, Fraternité Matin ran the headline “Kipré prône l’intégrisme religieux” (“Kipré advocates religious integrism”):
So many dangerous statements by the speaker, which can be considered integrist. Yet religious integrism is something Côte d’Ivoire has no use for.

Headline: Plume Libre, a Muslim paper born of multiparty politics
Text:
In October 1991 the first issue of Plume Libre appeared, an “Ivorian monthly of general news” run by young Muslim intellectuals. Its front page asked the question of the moment, “Islam in Côte d’Ivoire: what place?”, and already announced a feature on “origin” and “nationality”, “a peril for the Nation”. The editorial tied the paper to the growth of the private press:
One of the striking facts of the introduction of multiparty politics in Côte d’Ivoire has without doubt been the mass birth of newspapers, giving the written press a new dynamism.
By December, the paper was pointing to a double standard: Ronald Reagan, who had made 1983 “the year of the Bible”, was never called an integrist. “Had he been what you know, he would have been branded an integrist.”

Headline: Alif puts the word under scrutiny
Text:
In March 1992, the first issue of Alif devoted an article to the word now used to describe Muslims: “L’intégrisme : est-il l’apanage des seuls musulmans ?” (“Is integrism the preserve of Muslims alone?”). Its author, Djely, listed the provocative headlines of fellow papers, “Kipré prône l’intégrisme”, “L’intégrisme à nos portes” (“Integrism at our doors”), then traced the term’s Catholic genealogy:
Historically, the word “intégrisme” first appeared in 1892 in Spain, in the name of the integrist party founded by Candido Nocedal, an intransigent Catholic “who wanted to subordinate the state to the church”.
The same issue ran a headline on a “new crusade against Islam” after the Gulf War and followed the crisis in Algeria, where the army had just halted the electoral process won by the Islamic Salvation Front. Alif republished the feature in March 1995, at the height of the controversy.

Headline: Police break up the assembly at the Adjamé Great Mosque
Text:
On 28 November 1992, imams and delegations from across the country met at the Adjamé Great Mosque to found a new council, independent of the Conseil Supérieur Islamique (CSI) led by El Hadj Diaby Moustapha. The security forces dispersed them, on the grounds that the Minister of the Interior, Émile Constant Bombet, had not authorised the assembly. Two weeks later, Notre Temps described Muslims who “feel bullied, humiliated, marginalised”. In December, La Voie recalled how the minister had seen the initiative:
We still remember that the birth of this council, perceived by the Minister of the Interior, Mr Emile Constant Bombet, as a form of integrism of the Muslims of Côte d’Ivoire, nearly ended in tragedy on 28 November at the Adjamé great mosque.
Meeting in congress, the pupils and students of the AEEMCI backed the project.
Media Caption: Charles Bédé, “7ème congrès ordinaire de l’AEEMCI : le ‘oui’ des jeunes musulmans à la création du Conseil national islamique”, La Voie, 30 December 1992

Headline: The birth of the Conseil National Islamique
Text:
On 9 January 1993, the founding general assembly of the Conseil National Islamique (CNI) was finally held at the Adjamé Great Mosque, in the presence of imams, ministers and the associations behind the project. It elected imam Idriss Koudouss Koné as its president. Speaking at the assembly, imam Aboubacar Fofana denounced a double standard: when a Muslim talks politics, “he is branded an integrist”. Fraternité Matin reported his answer: “pious and sincere” Muslims “are quickly branded integrists”.
If being upright in managing public goods and in practising one’s faith means being an integrist, then all good Muslims are.
According to La Voie, he added that Muslims “are neither on the right nor on the left” and “cannot be manipulated”. Throughout the decade, the government would suspect the CNI of serving the opposition.
Media Caption: Souleymane T. Senn and Aristide Silué, “Assemblée générale constitutive du Conseil national islamique : Idriss Koné élu président”, La Voie, 11 January 1993

Headline: “Secular integrism”
Text:
In June 1993, the editorial of Plume Libre, signed by Dembélé Al Séni, turned the accusation against those who made it. “L’intégrisme laïc” described head teachers who wanted to see at school “neither caps, nor headscarves, still less veils”, and an administration where prayer beads and prayer mats “make the ‘secularists’ shudder”. Laïcité, he wrote, “is tending to establish itself as the ‘new single party’”.
Secular integrism, with its thousand ramifications and its more or less visible connections, now presents itself as one of the hardest scourges to fight.
The argument became a staple of the Islamic press: intolerance lay with a laïcité that excluded religion from public space.

Headline: Bédié: “it is wrong of some to call all Muslims…”
Text:
Félix Houphouët-Boigny died on 7 December 1993 and Henri Konan Bédié succeeded him. On 23 December, the new head of state received the representatives of the religious communities, including a CNI delegation led by imam Idriss Koudouss Koné. His speech, published by Fraternité Matin, combined reassurance and warning:
To be sincere, I want to tell you that it is wrong of some to describe all the Muslims of Côte d’Ivoire as integrists. On the contrary, I know that you and I are determined to fight excesses of every kind and to neutralise troublemakers everywhere.
In its letter of condolence, reprinted by Alif in January 1994, the CNI summed up the situation: “The old equation, Islam = fanaticism, invented, spread and imposed by medieval Europe, has now been replaced by: Islam = integrism.”

Headline: Fologo: integrism “stops at the gates of the Sahel”
Text:
On 12 March 1994, before thousands of supporters gathered at the sports ground in Treichville, Laurent Dona Fologo, secretary-general of the PDCI and Minister of National Integration, warned against two “diseases”. Plume Libre quoted his words:
There are two diseases that some want to bring into Côte d’Ivoire… the disease of regionalism and the disease of religious division (…) religious integrism stops at the gates of the Sahel; it does not enter the Ivorian forest.
For the paper, there was no need to “psychoanalyse” these words to understand that “the religion targeted here is Islam and the integrists singled out are the Muslims”. The geography of the speech made the Muslim, Sahelian north the gateway of the threat. The paper’s headline: “Muslims out!”
Media Caption: Dembélé Al Séni, “Meeting du PDCI le 12 Mars. Fologo : Musulmans Dehors !”, Plume Libre, April 1994

Headline: Tear gas in the mosques of Abobo
Text:
On Friday 10 June 1994, in the middle of prayers, police burst into the two adjoining mosques of Abobo Banco II to check residence permits. Tear-gas grenades and rifle butts left several people injured, including a woman of about 80; eleven people were detained. Imam El Hadj Diarra Sékou told La Voie:
Then uniformed police officers, wearing helmets with visors, burst into both mosques, batons and pistols in hand.
According to the worshippers, it was not the first raid. The Minister of Internal Security promised sanctions, and even Fraternité Matin reported the incident. The police raid on the Abobo Banco II mosque came to symbolise a central grievance of the period: treating Muslims as foreigners.
Media Caption: Freedom Neruda, Jean-Claude Ablet, César Etou and Séry Djaty, “Sacrilège et profanation à Abobo. Pour une histoire de carte de séjour : les policiers gazent des musulmans dans une mosquée”, La Voie, 11 June 1994

Headline: The electoral code and the “sub-Ivorians”
Text:
At the end of 1994, the new electoral code imposed nationality conditions on presidential candidates that the opposition read as aimed at Alassane Ouattara, a former prime minister, a Muslim and a northerner. Alif ran the headline “Code électoral : l’apartheid en Côte d’Ivoire” (“Electoral code: apartheid in Côte d’Ivoire”). Plume Libre saw in the speeches of the head of state and his ministers the search for an Ivorian “ethnic purity”:
Reserving Côte d’Ivoire for a “pure race” of Ivorians, thereby giving birth to sub-Ivorians who may vote but cannot stand for election.
With ivoirité, the line between Muslim, northerner and foreigner blurred, and the charge of integrism merged with the question of nationality.

Headline: “Good” and “bad” Muslims
Text:
After Houphouët-Boigny’s death, the government relied on the Conseil Supérieur Islamique (CSI) of El Hadj Diaby Moustapha, known as “Diaby Koweït”, whom La Voie accused as early as March 1994 of being backed by the new regime: “Which of the two councils to choose?”. In Fraternité Matin, Diaby declared himself “opposed to all forms of religious integrism”; three years later he added: “I am against all forms of integrism. I campaign for original Islam.” On 23 December 1994, Dr Balla Kéita, the president’s special adviser for cultural affairs, gave a lecture that the state daily headlined “integrism shall not pass”. The report summed up his message:
… to denounce the rise of religious integrism and intolerance promoted, in his view, by ambitious men who want to use religion to satisfy unavowed ambitions.
He said he felt “betrayed by certain CNI leaders who are working for the opposition”. The line was drawn: on one side a loyal Islam, on the other an Islam suspected of serving Alassane Ouattara.
Media Caption: Marie Chantal Ozoua, “Affaire Diaby Koweït contre CNI : du crétinisme provocateur au sacrilège offensant”, La Voie, 29 July 1994

Headline: “The government wants integrism”
Text:
On the night of 12 January 1995, armed men seized the car of the CNI president, Idriss Koudouss Koné. The government spoke of a mere car-jacking and condemned “the politicking and biased use” made of it by RFI and La Voie; the CNI spoke of an attempted abduction and denounced a will to “demonise it in order to disqualify it”. In La Voie, Gnaka Lagoké accused the regime of trying to push Muslims to breaking point:
Any reaction on their part would be regarded as a display of barbarity and Muslim integrism.
Integrism was no longer just an accusation: for the opposition, it was a trap set for a whole community in an election year.
Media Caption: Gnaka Lagoké, “Le pouvoir veut l’intégrisme”, La Voie, 16 January 1995

Headline: “We are not integrists”
Text:
In February 1995, the controversy spread through the whole press. In La Voie, Laurent Gbagbo, secretary-general of the FPI, stated: “I do not believe in religious integrism in Côte d’Ivoire”, and condemned the checks in mosques:
It is unacceptable to see police officers enter a mosque on the pretext of checking residence permits. It implies that, for these people, the word Muslim is synonymous with foreigner.
In Fraternité Matin, Venance Konan asked “Qui n’aime pas les musulmans ?” (“Who doesn’t like Muslims?”); La Voie replied with a list of grievances, from searches of places of prayer in Abobo and Treichville to the dismissal of Muslim officials. For the Night of Destiny, the CNI gathered the faithful at the Palais des Sports in Treichville on the theme “Islam: realities and prejudices in Côte d’Ivoire”. There, imam Aboubacar Samassi summed up the Muslims’ answer: “We are not integrists”.
Media Caption: Sylvain Hassan Boza, “Nuit du Destin : ‘Nous ne sommes pas des intégristes’ déclare l’imam Aboubakar Samassi”, Le Jour, 28 February 1995

Headline: Plume Libre’s journalists in prison
Text:
On 21 February 1995, the publication director of Plume Libre, Fousséni Dembélé, and the journalist Ibrahima Doumbia were arrested. On 2 March, they were sentenced to ten months in prison for “inciting disorder and tribal and religious hatred”. The next day, two journalists from La Patrie, a weekly close to the RDR, received a year for insulting the head of state. Le Jour asked: “Who is next?”. The Association des jeunes musulmans de Côte d’Ivoire responded:
The Rubicon has just been crossed in the trial of strength between the government and the Muslim community, with the arrest and sentencing of our brothers Dembelé Fousséni and Doumbia Ibrahima.
In April, a support committee held a night of prayer at the Adjamé great mosque for the “imprisoned” journalists.
Media Caption: Mory-Frey Touré, “La Patrie : un an de prison, Plume Libre : 10 mois. À qui le tour ?”, Le Jour, 6 March 1995

Headline: “Tribal and regional integrism”
Text:
In March 1995, Alif devoted a feature to the word integrism, recalled its Catholic origin, then turned the accusation against the government. Under the headline “L’intégrisme tribal et régional”, the paper published the list of chief executives, directors and chiefs of staff serving in the presidency, the ministries, customs, the Treasury and even Fraternité Matin, to suggest that the key posts went to the same groups; the list continued in April. In the same issue, Yéo Marouf concluded:
If there is an integrism in Côte d’Ivoire, it is indeed a tribal and regional integrism.
Tribalism became the reverse of integrism: the real danger, these papers argued, was the ethnic exclusion practised at the top of the state.

Headline: “Let us preserve our populations from integrism”
Text:
At the end of his tour of the north-west, from 6 to 9 July 1995, President Henri Konan Bédié addressed the people of Touba. He named two dangers: giving a partisan meaning to religious affiliation, and integrism, which was “admittedly not yet a direct threat to Côte d’Ivoire”. Fraternité Matin made it the headline of its report:
It is the scourge of integrism, whose followers turn a religion of peace into an instrument of death… We must preserve our populations from it.
Delivered in a predominantly Muslim region, three months before a presidential election from which Alassane Ouattara would be excluded, the warning implicitly likened the northern opposition to the Islamist insurgencies then bloodying Algeria.

Headline: A presidential election under strain
Text:
In October 1995, the opposition united in the Front républicain called for an “active boycott” of an election from which Alassane Ouattara, “ostracised by the electoral code”, was excluded. Demonstrations were put down. On 2 October in Abobo, after dispersing protesters, gendarmes smashed the window of a house next to a mosque and threw in a tear-gas grenade: “Another mosque gassed”, ran the headline in La Voie. On the eve of the vote of 22 October, imams, pastors and bishops issued a joint appeal:
We, that is, a group of religious leaders, imams, Protestant pastors and Catholic bishops, having met in long consultation, come to tell you, in the name of the one God, living and merciful, who never abandons those who call on him in sincerity and faith, that we refuse war and its dark consequences once and for all.
Henri Konan Bédié was elected without a serious opponent.
Media Caption: César Etou, “Encore une mosquée gazée”, La Voie, 3 October 1995

Headline: From the “integrist” label to ivoirité
Text:
After 1995 the word appeared less often in the press, but the label remained. In July 1997, at the Mawlid celebrations, imam Idriss Koudouss Koné denounced those who had tried “to stick the label ‘integrism’ on the leaders of the COSIM and the CNI”. In November 1999, as Alassane Ouattara’s nationality was being challenged, imam Aboubacar Fofana, spokesman of the COSIM, opened his interview with Le Jour, his hand on the Qur’an, with a profession of identity:
I am Ivorian, born of a father and mother who were themselves Ivorian by birth.
The paper summed up his message: the excesses of ivoirité were leading “to a hunt for Muslims and the people of the north”, driven by “a political integrism that blocks every path to dialogue”. The word had changed sides.
Media Caption: Abdoulaye Sangaré and Jean-Roche Kouamé, “L’imam Aboubacar Fofana : ‘Nous demandons au gouvernement de faire attention’”, Le Jour, 16 November 1999

Headline: Mosques burned, imams murdered
Text:
The coup of December 1999 did not end the suspicion. On the eve of the presidential election of October 2000, from which Ouattara was again excluded, the Muslim hierarchy denounced the summoning of imams to the gendarmerie and searches without warrant “in some twenty mosques in Abidjan”, aimed at worshippers suspected of supporting Ouattara. In December, the violence targeted places of worship directly. In a statement published by Le Patriote, the CNI reported:
On 5 December 2000, at about 8.30 a.m., a group of students claiming to belong to the FESCI attacked the Abobo Sogefina mosque. After breaking down the doors, they set it on fire with burning tyres.
After the outbreak of war in 2002, the COSIM denounced the attack on the great mosque of Agboville and the murder of several imams and preachers, including imam Mahmoud Samassi.
Media Caption: “Conseil national islamique : les exactions commises contre les mosquées et les musulmans par les forces de l’ordre”, Le Patriote, 11 December 2000

Headline: Integrism, radicalism, jihadism
Text:
After 2002, integrism almost disappeared from the Ivorian press in the collection: the threat was now called terrorism and jihadism. In June 2013, as the war in Mali raised fears of contagion, imam Mamadou Dosso, secretary-general of the CNI, judged the threat “probable” in socio-political terms. Yet he repeated the argument that Muslim intellectuals had opposed to the word integrism twenty years earlier: the problem was born of politics.
Radicalism, also called integrism or jihadism, arises from the partisan management by the public authorities of religious practices and of the hold of religions over society.
The next day, Le Jour Plus reported the arrest of six imams in the “hunt for jihadists”. Alassane Ouattara had then been president since 2011.
Media Caption: Abou Traoré, “Imam Dosso Mamadou, secrétaire général du conseil national islamique (Cni) à propos de la menace Djihadiste : ‘Voici pourquoi la Côte d’Ivoire est dans le viseur des Djihadistes’”, Le Jour Plus, 10 June 2013

Headline: Grand-Bassam: “Hand in hand, we will defeat terrorism”
Text:
On 13 March 2016, the Grand-Bassam attack, claimed by al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb, struck Côte d’Ivoire. Muslim organisations condemned it at once. Islam Info published the reactions of the president of the COSIM, Cheick Aïma Boikary Fofana, alongside those of the Catholic bishops, under the headline “Hand in hand, we will defeat terrorism!”:
The miracle could not last any longer. Our country was an exception to the battlefield coveted by the terrorists, or by all those whom our country’s new image of dazzling prosperity could and was bound to disturb after such a serious crisis.
Twenty years after the quarrel over integrism, the threat had changed its name, and it was Muslim leaders who called for national unity. The chart of “scary” terms in the press on this page follows the shift from integrism to terrorism.
